title: Bash
subtitle: The shell that runs on almost every server and laptop: commands, quoting and expansions, pipes, scripts, text processing and safe automation, from a first command to professional practice.
description: Bash, the Bourne-Again SHell, is the GNU Project's command interpreter, first released by Brian Fox in 1989 as a free replacement for the Unix Bourne shell. It is the default interactive shell on most Linux systems, it is what most shell scripts are written for, and it is the language of countless build scripts, deployment pipelines, container entry points, CI jobs and one-off automations. Knowing it well means being at home on any server and being able to glue programs together in a few lines.

This course is for anyone who knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. It starts with what a shell and a terminal are and how a command line is read, works through quoting and expansions (the part of Bash that surprises everyone), pipes and redirection, conditionals, loops, functions and arrays, then the classic text tools (grep, sed, awk, sort and friends), and ends with writing scripts that fail safely, checking them with ShellCheck, managing processes and jobs, and a complete automation project.

Bash comes with almost every Linux distribution. On macOS the built-in Bash is a very old version (3.2), so install a current one with a package manager such as Homebrew, or use the default zsh for interactive work and Bash for scripts; on Windows, use the Windows Subsystem for Linux or Git Bash. The source and documentation are at [gnu.org/software/bash](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/). There is no official online playground, but [ShellCheck](https://www.shellcheck.net/) checks scripts in the browser. Every complete script in these lessons was run with GNU Bash 5.1 and the GNU core utilities by Lumenary's test suite, and the output shown is the output it printed; the lessons point out features added in Bash 5.2 and 5.3. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: What a shell and a terminal are, how Bash reads a command line, quoting and the expansions that happen before any command runs, and connecting programs with pipes and redirection.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: Exit statuses, conditionals and loops; functions, arguments and arrays in real scripts; and answering questions about data with grep, sed, awk, sort and the other classic text tools.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: Write scripts that fail safely and pass ShellCheck, manage processes, jobs and signals, and build a complete automation script the way professionals do.
